passages.text: ATG16L1 rs2241880/T300A increases susceptibility to perianal Crohn's disease: An updated meta-analysis on inflammatory bowel disease risk and clinical outcomes  ATG16L1 rs2241880/T300A increases susceptibility to perianal Crohn's disease: an updated meta-analysis on inflammatory bowel disease risk and clinical outcomes
Abstract
Background

ATG16L1 plays a fundamental role in the degradative intracellular pathway known as autophagy, being a mediator of inflammation and microbial homeostasis. The variant rs2241880 can diminish these capabilities, potentially contributing to inflammatory bowel disease (IBD) pathogenesis.
Objectives

To perform an updated meta-analysis on the association between ATG16L1 rs2241880 and IBD susceptibility by exploring the impact of age, ethnicity, and geography. Moreover, to investigate the association between rs2241880 and clinical features.
Methods

Literature searches up until September 2022 across 7 electronic public databases were performed for all case-control studies on ATG16L1 rs2241880 and IBD. Pooled odds ratios (ORP) and 95% CI were calculated under the random effects model.
Results

Our analyses included a total of 30,606 IBD patients, comprising 21,270 Crohn's disease (CD) and 9336 ulcerative colitis (UC) patients, and 33,329 controls. ATG16L1 rs2241880 was significantly associated with CD susceptibility, where the A allele was protective (ORP: 0.74, 95% CI: 0.72-0.77, p-value: <0.001), while the G allele was a risk factor (ORP: 1.23, 95% CI: 1.09-1.39, p-value: 0.001), depending on the minor allele frequencies observed in this multi-ancestry study sample. rs2241880 was predominantly relevant in Caucasians from North America and Europe, and in Latin American populations. Importantly, CD patients harbouring the G allele were significantly more predisposed to perianal disease (ORP: 1.21, 95% CI: 1.07-1.38, p-value: 0.003).
Conclusions

ATG16L1 rs2241880 (G allele) is a consistent risk factor for IBD in Caucasian cohorts and influences clinical outcomes. As its role in non-Caucasian populations remains ambiguous, further studies in under-reported populations are necessary.
Key summary
ATG16L1 rs2241880/T300A is a predisposition locus for Crohn's disease; however, the susceptibility pattern is not universal, especially in non-Caucasian populations.
The locus has been linked to predisposition for the ileal subphenotype of Crohn's disease, but not any other biomarker, clinical phenotype, or outcome of inflammatory bowel disease.
Summarise the established knowledge on this subject
ATG16L1 rs2241880 has relevance as a biomarker for Crohn's disease in Caucasians, particularly from North America and Europe, as well as in populations of Latin American ancestry.
Clinically, rs2241880 influences predisposition to Crohn's disease associated perianal disease.

As ATG16L1 rs2241880 can influence predisposition to perianal disease, this study provides a better understanding of the pathogenesis, with the potential to identify at-risk patients and initiate disease surveillance resulting in more effective treatment.
What are the significant and/or new findings of this study?
INTRODUCTION

Inflammatory bowel disease (IBD) describes the collection of chronic and relapsing inflammatory disorders afflicting the gastrointestinal (GI) tract, whereby there is an absence of a discernible aetiological agent or clear underlying cellular process contributing to inflammation. The two predominant clinical manifestations of IBD are Crohn's disease (CD), and ulcerative colitis (UC). Typical symptoms suffered by patients include diarrhoea, abdominal cramps, rectal bleeding, weight loss and fatigue. The occurrence of extraintestinal manifestations (EIM) is not uncommon, potentially affecting the musculoskeletal, dermatological, ocular, oral, metabolic, and renal systems.

In 2017, it was estimated that there were more than 6.8 million people globally living with IBD, and the age-standardised prevalence rate sat at 79.5 per 100,000. Traditionally, IBD has been labelled as a Western disease, as the highest incidence and prevalence rates have been consistently reported in North America and Europe. However, an epidemiological shift over the past decades has seen the emergence of IBD as a global disease with rapidly increasing incidence rates in newly industrialised or 'westernised' regions such as South America, Asia, and Africa. The impact of ethnicity on the risk of IBD remains somewhat elusive due to the paucity of data in non-Caucasian populations, although current evidence suggests that non-Hispanic Caucasians are the most at risk of developing IBD in their lifetime.

The aetiology of IBD remains largely enigmatic due to its complexity and the lack of an identifiable cause-and-effect relationship. As a multifactorial disorder, IBD is hypothesised to stand firmly at the crossroads between host genetic susceptibility, an aberrant immune response, the gut microbiota (both commensal and pathogenic), and environmental interactions (e.g., diet and smoking).

The pursuit to identify those host genetic factors that are implicated in IBD susceptibility remains heavily focussed on immunogenetics, including microbial recognition. Over the years, GWAS studies have identified some 200 IBD susceptibility loci. An early candidate in IBD GWAS studies was rs2241880 (A > G, also known as T300A), situated in the autophagy-related protein 16-like 1 (ATG16L1) locus. ATG16L1 plays a fundamental role in the degradative intracellular pathway known as autophagy. Autophagy is critical for the maintenance of overall cellular homeostasis, especially during periods of nutrient starvation, as it is involved in the recycling of old or damaged organelles and proteins. Autophagy can also be directed towards the eradication of pathogens, rendering it an important component of the innate immune response, intimately linked to inflammation through its influence on inflammatory cells (i.e., macrophages, lymphocytes, and neutrophils) and modulation of pro-inflammatory cytokine production. ATG16L1 rs2241880 is a missense substitution at position 300 on the polypeptide (Threonine to Alanine), altering protein polarity and susceptibility to caspase-3 degradation, which is suspected to contribute to abnormal autophagic functions. Consequently, autophagy, one of the principal mechanisms by which the host can maintain intestinal homeostasis, both immunologically and microbially, is defective and potentially contributes to IBD pathogenesis.

Previous meta-analyses have been published on the matter; however, these have generally only focussed on an association with CD susceptibility. What we present here, thus, is the most comprehensive meta-analysis to date on the association of ATG16L1 rs2241880 and IBD, including both CD and UC, determining any relevant demographic susceptibility patterns based on age (paediatric vs. adult), ethnicity (Caucasian, East Asian, South Asian, Middle Eastern, Latin American), and geographical origin (Northern Europe, Eastern Europe, Southern Europe, Western Europe, North America, South America, Oceania, Middle East, East Asia, South Asia). Importantly, we attempted to associate rs2241880 with relevant clinical features and outcomes including disease location, disease behaviour, presence of perianal disease and presence of extraintestinal manifestations (EIM).
METHODS
Literature search strategy and screening

This study was conducted using the Preferred Reporting Items for Systematic Review and Meta-Analysis protocols (PRISMA) with a systematic literature search conducted independently by two authors (IS & NCR). Any discrepancies in study selection or data collection were discussed between the authors to reach a consensus. A systematic search of publicly available scientific literature databases (Pubmed, Science Direct, Scopus, Web of Science, Cochrane, Lilacs and Scielo) was conducted up until 30 September 2022. The search terms utilised are presented in Supplementary Table S1. Retrievals were also identified through hand-searching and manual review of reference lists from selected articles. Articles were initially screened based on title, keywords and abstract to identify records of relevance.
Study selection criteria
Inclusion criteria

Full text articles were selected for eligibility based on the following inclusion criteria: (1) full original peer-reviewed article available (no abstracts or conference articles) in either English, Spanish or Portuguese, (2) a clear case-control study design with a diagnosis of IBD (CD and UC) denoted as 'cases', and (3) population-based or hospital-based controls denoted as healthy or otherwise (non-IBD), (4) paediatric (early-onset) or adult populations, (5) study evaluates the association of polymorphism with any IBD outcome or phenotype, and (6) accessibility to raw data (genotypic and allelic frequencies).
Exclusion criteria
Studies were excluded (1) should their methodology include familial (related) data, (2) presence of duplicated data, and (3) the control group deviated from Hardy-Weinberg Equilibrium (HWE).
Study quality assessment and data extraction

To further assess eligibility and quality of the full-text selected articles, the Newcastle-Ottawa Scale (NOS) Score was implemented using the standard 9-point system. Studies were judged based on subject selection, comparability of subject groups (cases and controls), and the ascertainment of exposure (genotyping). The final selected studies were extracted for author, year, journal, geographical location, ethnicity, age category (adult or paediatric (early-onset) population), total genotype numbers, and ATG16L1 rs2241880 genotypic (if applicable) and allelic frequencies.

For those articles which also performed genotype-phenotype correlations, genotypic/allelic data were extracted and stratified by one or more of the following variables: Montreal/Vienna classification (disease location and disease behaviour), presence of EIM, or perianal disease. Corresponding authors were contacted if studies indicated such analyses were conducted but data was not accessible/shown.
Statistical analysis

The pooled odds ratio (ORP) was calculated using the generic inverse variance method where the OR from each individual study was weighted by the inverse of their variance. The random-effects model was employed to calculate ORp and 95% confidence intervals (CI) to account for the assumed variation in the true effects due to study-level heterogeneity, which is summarised by estimating the mean and variance of a distribution of true effects. A meta-regression was also performed to assess the impact of multiple independent variables on the effect size, allowing us to identify potential sources of heterogeneity or confounding variables influencing the association between ATG16L1 rs2241880 and CD. The variables included in the regression model were ethnicity (Caucasian, East Asian, South Asian, Middle Eastern, Latin American), age of onset (paediatric vs. adult) and study NOS score (<=5 vs. >= 6). Stratified analyses were further conducted based on the age of onset, ethnicity, geographical origin (Northern Europe, Eastern Europe, Southern Europe, Western Europe, North America, South America, Oceania, Middle East, East Asia, South Asia) and study NOS score. To test for heterogeneity, the Cochran's-Q test was applied, where a p-value <0.1 was suggestive of heterogeneity. Since some of the stratified analyses comprised only a small number of studies, which ultimately undermined the power of the Cochran's-Q test, the Higgins test (I 2) was also employed in parallel for all analyses. The Higgins test defines the percentage of total variation across all studies due to heterogeneity rather than chance, such that I  2  lies between 0% and 100%, where 0% indicates the absence of heterogeneity and increasing values indicate greater heterogeneity. The following categories for I  2  values were assigned: low heterogeneity: <25%, moderate heterogeneity: 25%-75% and high heterogeneity: >75%. To further identify influential studies and examine statistical robustness, leave-one-out sensitivity analysis was performed. To assess for potential publication bias, funnel plots were generated, and Egger's regression asymmetry tests were conducted. All statistical tests were carried out as two-tailed, with a p-value of <0.05 deemed statistically significant. All statistical analyses were conducted using the Comprehensive Meta-Analysis (CMA) Software package V. 4.0 (Biostat, Englewood, New Jersey). Genotype-phenotype correlation analysis was further controlled via the application of the FDR method (Benjamini-Hochberg) at level alpha (0.05) using an available online tool (https://tools.carbocation.com/FDR).
RESULTS
Literature search and study characteristics

Our systematic search of seven publicly available scientific literature databases revealed collective 5891 records across all search terms used (Figure 1). Hand-searching yielded an additional 9 articles, totalling 5900 records. After duplicate removal, 520 records remained. Initial screening of title, keywords and abstracts, and application of our inclusion criteria, led to 83 studies for qualitative analysis using the NOS Scoring system. We ascertained a total of 61 studies for data extraction and inclusion in the quantitative meta-analysis, consisting of 30,606 IBD cases (21,270 CD and 9336 UC), and 33,329 controls. Reasoning for the exclusion of articles at the data extraction stage is highlighted in Supplementary Table S2. The final selected studies and their general characteristics as well as allele and/or genotype frequencies are presented in Tables 1 and 2 for CD and UC, respectively.

Study quality

By employing the NOS Scoring system, we determined that the overall quality of studies included in the quantitative meta-analysis was high with the majority (47/61; 77%) attaining >=6 stars. In special circumstances where a single study reported on multiple independent cohorts, a NOS score was applied for each independent cohort, and the final NOS score for the article was determined by averaging the score of those cohorts.
Association of ATG16L1 rs221880 and IBD

To preface, each population was evaluated to determine the minor allele, G or A, using their respective control cohort, and grouped accordingly for the following analyses. This was done to account for the genetic variations between both ethnic and geographical populations, as evidenced by public databases (International HapMap Project), which report that the frequency of the A allele is 0.458 in European (Caucasian) samples, 0.830 in Japanese (East Asian) samples, and 0.611 in Han Chinese (East Asian) samples.

Our unique approach in segregating the study populations based on the minor allele frequency (MAF) in their respective controls provides consideration of the genetic effects on population differentiation across diverse ethnic groups. It is well known that human allele frequencies of single nucleotide polymorphisms (SNPs) diverge based on geography and ethnicity, which is influenced by several factors including natural selection, whereby the selective pressures of environmental conditions can modulate the allelic balance across populations. In addition, except in instances of Mendelian diseases, the role of the minor allele in complex diseases has a natural tendency to be inherently attributed to be the risk allele. Furthermore, association tests were reported more likely to be statistically significant if the minor allele in the population was considered the risk allele instead of the major allele. Notwithstanding, the major allele may of course be recognised as the risk allele in certain populations, as was the case in the current meta-analysis, which identified that almost half of the included study populations harbours the ATG16L1 rs2241880 risk allele (G) as the major allele in their respective controls. By conducting the analyses independently for each allele and population, based on their respective MAF, we can provide a neutral evaluation of the role of rs2241880 in IBD. In this respect, analysis for CD and UC susceptibility will be presented for each allele independently.
Effect of ATG16L1 rs2241880 A allele on CD susceptibility

Populations with the rs2241880 minor allele denoted as A included 33 independent case-control studies across 30 articles (Figure 2a). Overall, ORP was determined to be a highly significant 0.74 (0.72-0.77; p-value: <0.001) under the random effects model, indicating that the A allele is favourable against CD development (Figure 2a). There was no evidence of heterogeneity in this analysis (Figure 2a).

Forest plots of the meta-analysis assessing the association between ATG16L1 rs2241880 CD susceptibility. (a) Analysis in respect to the A allele. (b) Analysis in respect to the G allele. Pooled odds ratios (ORP) with 95% confidence intervals (CI) were calculated under the random effects model (coloured diamond). Squares denote the contributing weight of each study to analyses. Q, Cochran's Q test, I  2 ; Higgins test.

A meta-regression for the A allele in CD included 27 studies in the model since 6 studies were excluded from this analysis due to missing data for one or more independent variables. The regression model showed that these variables (ethnicity, age of onset, and study NOS score) did not influence the overall association between the A allele and CD susceptibility (p-value: 0.623, Supplementary Table S3). However, as the magnitude of the effect size can still differ based on some of these variables, we also conducted stratified analyses.

Limiting included studies in these analyses to those of the highest quality (n = 26, study NOS score >=6) did not influence the significance nor effect size of the A allele on CD susceptibility (OR: 0.75, 95% CI: 0.72-0.78, p-value <0.001; data not shown).

The onset of IBD can occur at any point within a lifetime, where paediatric-onset IBD (before the age of 16) is often treated as a separate entity from that of adult-onset IBD due to differences in clinical presentation and the natural course of disease. On this account, we evaluated the effect of rs2241880 in the context of age onset, broadly, adult-onset versus paediatric-onset. The A allele reported a highly significant ORP of 0.74 (0.71-0.77; p-value: <0.001) and 0.77 (0.68-0.87; p-value: <0.001) for CD adult-onset and paediatric onset, respectively (Table 3). Heterogeneity was detected only in the paediatric-onset subgroup (I  2 : 40.14%) (Table 3).
Pooled effect size and heterogeneity for the meta-analyses assessing the association between the ATG16L1 rs2241880 A allele and IBD susceptibility.

Our approach to evaluating the impact of ethnicity on rs2241880 and IBD susceptibility involved categorising each population crudely into Caucasian, East Asian, South Asian, Middle Eastern and Latin American categories. When stratified by ethnicity, only populations of Caucasian and Middle Eastern ancestry appeared to harbour the A allele as the minor allele (Table 3). Stratification by ethnicity revealed relevance for the A allele in CD susceptibility only in Caucasian cohorts, with a highly significant ORP of 0.75 (0.72-0.78, p-value: <0.001) (Table 3). No heterogeneity was found (I  2 : 0.00%) in both subgroups (Table 3).

It is clear in genetic association studies, including this one, that the impact of susceptibility variants not only vary across ethnicities but also across geographical regions of the same ethnicity. To this end, we also investigated the impact of geographical origin on rs2241880 and IBD risk to determine any susceptibility patterns. Populations were stratified according to the following geographical regions: Northern Europe, Eastern Europe, Southern Europe, Western Europe, North America, South America, Oceania, Middle East, East Asia, South Asia. This categorisation was conducted in line with the United Nations geoscheme for regions and individual countries.

Given our findings in the ethnicity-stratified analysis, unsurprisingly, we found a pattern where those populations with the A allele as the minor allele were concentrated in regions of the globe with a majority Caucasian ethnicity (Europe and North America). The A allele was a highly significant protective factor across all of Europe (Table 3). Furthermore, the A allele held the most protective value in North America with an ORP of 0.67 (0.61-0.74, p-value: <0.001). No significant evidence of heterogeneity was reported across all subgroups, except Southern Europe, which showed the presence of moderate heterogeneity (I  2 : 34.50%). In summary, the A allele appears to have significant relevance in Caucasian ethnic groups, from both the North American and European regions, which confers protection against CD development.
Effect of ATG16L1 rs2241880G allele on CD susceptibility

Populations with the rs2241880 minor allele denoted as G included 33 independent case-control studies across 31 articles (Figure 2b). For CD, the G allele showed a significant ORP of 1.23 (1.09-1.36, p-value: 0.001) (Figure 2b). There was a high level of heterogeneity noted in this analysis (I  2 : 82.67% (Figure 2b).

A meta-regression for the G allele in CD included 29 studies in the model since 4 studies were excluded due to missing data for one or more of the independent variables included (age of onset and study NOS score). Ethnicity was not included in the model due to colinearity. The regression model showed that neither of these independent variables influenced the overall association between the G allele and CD susceptibility (p-value: 0.36; Supplementary Table S3). However, given that the magnitude of the effect size can still differ based on some of these variables, we also conducted stratified analyses.

Stratification based on high study quality (n = 25, study NOS score >=6) did not undermine the association between the G allele and CD, still reaching a highly significant OR of 1.22 (95% CI: 1.06-1.41, p-value: 0.007; data not shown).

Following stratification by age, the G allele was shown to be a highly significant risk factor in both adult-onset and paediatric-onset CDs. The ORP for adult-onset was reported to be 1.19 (1.06-1.34, p-value: 0.003), while the ORP for paediatric-onset was reported to be 1.47 (1.12-1.95, p-value: 0.006) (Table 4). Moderate levels of heterogeneity were reported for both adult-onset and paediatric-onset analyses (I  2 : 72.67% and I  2 : 55.11%, respectively, Table 4).
Pooled effect size and heterogeneity for the meta-analyses assessing the association between the ATG16L1 rs2241880 G allele and IBD susceptibility.

Effect of ATG16L1 rs2241880 on UC susceptibility

Our analyses on the impact of rs2241880 on UC susceptibility revealed largely negligible effects in both allelic analysis (Tables 3 and 4; Supplementary materials) and across all analysis types. Thus, no further analysis (clinic manifestations) was conducted on the UC populations.
Effect of ATG16L1 rs2241880 on clinical manifestation and outcomes of CD

The clinical manifestation of IBD is highly heterogeneous, and the potential for accurate molecular diagnosis and prognosis has always remained a lucrative clinical application. Here, we attempted to evaluate the applicability of ATG16L1 rs2241880 as a biomarker of different clinical features and outcomes of CD. This included disease location (ileum involvement vs. no ileum involvement), disease behaviour (only inflammatory (i.e., non-stricturing and non-penetrating) versus. stricturing or penetrating), presence of perianal disease, or EIM. As confirmed in the meta-analysis, the G allele is the risk allele and as such, all our genotype-phenotype analyses were conducted with the A allele as reference.

A significant clinical outcome of CD is perianal disease which can be characterised by inflammation and injury at or near the anus, including fistulae, abscesses, and skin tags. Stratification based on the presence or absence of perianal disease included 860 and 1720 patients, respectively, across seven independent case-control studies. Here, we identified a significant association with increased susceptibility to perianal disease in CD patients carrying the G risk allele (ORP: 1.21, 95% CI: 1.07-1.38, adjusted p-value: 0.003, Table 5.) with an adjusted p-value of 0.015 after FDR correction (Benjamini-Hochberg). The remaining comparisons failed to yield any significant role for the G allele with other clinical manifestations (Table 5).

Sensitivity analysis and publication bias

Both the ATG16L1 rs2241880 A and G allele remained a statistically significant risk factor for CD irrespective of what cohort was removed from the analysis each time. Statistical significance for the impact of an allele in UC susceptibility is lost when six out of the 18 studies are removed in the random effects model. This is most likely a by-product of the weak association observed. The G allele is not significantly associated with UC irrespective of what study was removed at a time. The significance of the G allele in CD associated perianal disease associated is achieved irrespective of which paper was removed for sensitivity analysis, inferring robustness. There was no evidence of publication bias in these meta-analyses, except in the G allele analysis for CD susceptibility (p-value: 0.008, Supplementary Table S4, Figures S1-S4).
DISCUSSION

As one of the first identified susceptibility loci from GWAS studies, ATG16L1 rs2241880 has since provided conflicting evidence over its inclusion and applicability in the molecular profile of IBD susceptibility. To the best of the authors' knowledge, the last meta-analysis conducted on this topic was in 2017, and since then several more studies have been reported including those in understudied or minority populations, contributing to the growing literature on the impact of rs2241880 in the pathogenesis of IBD. Thus, we sought to provide an updated, comprehensive meta-analysis of the available literature on ATG16L1 rs2241880 on IBD susceptibility. Moreover, we aimed to identify any trends in clinical presentation of CD as well as attributable susceptibility demographics (age, ethnicity, or geography).

Our meta-analysis involved a total of 30,606 IBD patients, comprising 21,270 CD patients and 9336 UC patients, and 33,329 controls, across 68 populations from 61 different articles: the largest meta-analysis on this subject to date. We present a confirmation of the highly significant association of ATG16L1 rs2241880 with CD susceptibility, and to a lesser extent with UC susceptibility. The A allele was determined to be protective against CD with an ORP of 0.74 (0.72-0.77), and complementarily, the G allele was determined to be a risk factor with an ORP of 1.23 (1.09-1.39). With regard to UC susceptibility, we report only an association with the A allele, which holds a very mild protective value with an ORP of 0.95 (0.90-1.00).

While early-onset and adult-onset IBD may carry differing underlying pathogenesis, we report here that rs2241880 contributes significantly to CD development, regardless of age of onset. Compared to adult-onset, in early-onset IBD genetic predisposition is suspected to carry greater influence in aetiology due to the more limited exposure to environmental risk factors. This is reflected in our finding that the G allele held a higher OR for paediatric-onset CD compared with adult-onset CD (ORP: 1.47 vs. 1.18).

The influence of ethnicity on IBD phenotype and outcomes has been demonstrated across Caucasians, Blacks, Hispanics, and Asians. Whether this is attributed to true differences in genetics, or rather environmental and lifestyle factors coupled with socioeconomic disparities, is yet to be clearly established. As described previously, the genetic implication of ethnic diversity plays a major role in establishing the validity of such genetic markers in complex diseases such as IBD. The current literature describes a lack of a universal susceptibility pattern for ATG16L1 rs2241880 in IBD pathogenesis. With the incidence rates of IBD varying greatly between different ethnic groups, it is conceivable to credit this, at least in part, to the differences in allele frequencies of disease-associated SNPs. The current meta-analysis demonstrates almost exclusive relevance in Caucasian cohorts, and more specifically in high-risk 'Westernised' regions (North America and Europe). Interestingly, Caucasian populations displayed great variability in the assignment of the minor allele, while Asian populations largely remained undivided (i.e., the minor allele was almost always designated as G). This would suggest that despite being a risk allele, the rs2241880 G allele may evolutionarily serve a homeostatic purpose. Furthermore, the lower G allele frequency in East Asian populations coincides with a lower rate of IBD incidence rates. We also present evidence, for the first time, of the relevance of ATG16L1 rs2241880 (G) allele in CD development in patients from Latin American populations, which failed to be achieved by single studies.

Importantly, a novel significant association between rs2241880 and perianal disease was identified in the current meta-analysis. The manifestation of perianal disease in the clinical course of CD is commonly reported in 25%-80% of patients. The literature is increasingly supporting an underlying genetic predisposition to the development of perianal fistulae. Our findings indicate that rs2241880 is a part of this susceptibility profile, as CD patients harbouring the G allele were found to be at increased risk of developing perianal disease (Table 5; ORP: 1.21, 95% CI: 1.07-1.38). ATG16L1 is not the first member of the autophagic pathway to be associated with perianal disease, as variants in another key autophagy protein, IRGM (rs4958847 and rs1000113), were associated with perianal fistulas in an Italian population. Due to the role of autophagy in mediating inflammation, hinderance of the function of these proteins could lead to aberrant inflammation, conducive to perianal disease.

On the contrary to the above findings for CD, our conclusions for the significance of rs2241880 on UC susceptibility are more unassuming. A very modest protective relationship was established for the A allele, which was restricted to adult-onset UC (Table 3). Notably, we observed a significant protective role for the A allele in UC susceptibility for Caucasians from Western Europe (Table 3). With larger sample sizes available from these regions, it does set a precedent for the numbers required to fully illustrate the more limited role of rs2241880 in UC susceptibility. Differences in the pathophysiology between CD and UC are suspected to dictate the relevance of rs2241880 in their susceptibility. While the influence of genetic predisposition is viewed to lesser magnitude in UC pathogenesis, disease-specific risk loci do exist for UC such as ECM1, yet the impact of ethnicity is again pronounced.

Most case-control studies underscore a modest contribution of ATG16L1 rs2241880 to IBD susceptibility which is undermined by the lack of statistical power. The current meta-analysis is able to overcome this obstacle to provide a more comprehensive examination of the role of rs2241880 in IBD susceptibility. We are acutely aware of potential population stratification in these analyses due to the ethnic bias of Caucasian populations prevalent in the majority of these studies, which is more than likely driving some significance. We attempted to circumvent these issues by stratifying not only by ethnicity but also by geographical origin. Further, a drawback of meta-analyses is the often-high level of heterogeneity reported, which is a natural and routine phenomenon in meta-analyses involving population studies due to their clinical and methodological differences. The majority of the included studies had a NOS score between 6 and 8. The main study limitation noted within individual studies was a lack of specificity on the definition and selection of controls. Further, study design varied greatly, with almost 90% of studies not age- and gender-matching their controls during recruitment, which undermines their comparability. Beyond any clinical or methodological differences between studies, publication bias could also be a contributing factor, as was noted for the analyses for the G allele in CD susceptibility (p-value: 0.008), which also carried high levels of heterogeneity (I  2 : 82.67%, p-value: 0.000). By carefully implementing a NOS scoring system, applying the random effects model, a dual test of heterogeneity (Cochran's Q-statistic and I  2 -statistic), and performing a meta-regression, we endeavoured to minimise subjectivity and the effects of heterogeneity but cannot entirely exclude residual biases. In addition, we note other limitations in our approach of this meta-analysis; (1) not all studies clearly denoted what minor allele they were reporting on, and (2) some of the stratified analyses were constrained due to limited statistical power. More epidemiological data on IBD incidence in understudied populations and ethnicities (African, Latin American) are needed to supplement the findings here, as the current data is still too heavily saturated in Western regions (North America and Europe). We also cannot ignore environmental influence and its role in the increasing rates of IBD in these new regions, which has been deemed too fast in the past 60 years to be purely explained by changes in the genetic make-up of these populations.

To summarise, we provide increasing evidence for the use of ATG16L1 rs2241880 as a clinical biomarker in IBD susceptibility and clinical outcomes, especially for patients of Caucasian ethnicities residing in North America and Europe, and those of Latin American ancestry. The G allele remains a significant risk factor for CD susceptibility, whereas the A allele illustrates a protective role in both CD and UC development. Due to the large number of studies and patients included, we provide novel insights into the role of rs2241880 on the clinical features of CD, that earlier meta-analyses failed to achieve which includes a significant role for the G allele in the predisposition to perianal disease.

passages.text: Matrix Gla Protein, a New Target Fighting Against Fibrosis of Nonalcoholic Steatohepatitis?

Nonalcoholic fatty liver disease (NAFLD, now also called metabolic dysfunction-associated steatotic liver disease [MASLD]) is a chronic liver disease linked to obesity and type 2 diabetes, affecting 30% of the global population. Nonalcoholic steatohepatitis (NASH), its severe form, can lead to cirrhosis or hepatocellular carcinoma. One strategy to reduce liver-related mortality is to prevent the progression of fibrogenesis, because hepatic fibrosis severity is one of the strongest prognostic indicators in chronic liver diseases, particularly NASH. Liver fibrosis is a complex process involving progressive accumulation of extracellular matrix (ECM) components, alterations in ECM degradation, and distortion of liver parenchyma in response to chronic damage. Fibrogenesis is driven primarily by the activation of hepatic stellate cells (HSCs), causing increased deposition of fibrillar ECM that negatively affects regeneration of the liver parenchyma over time. Subsequently, identifying new targets to halt or reverse liver fibrogenesis holds promise as a possible treatment for NASH.

The course of NAFLD varies owing to genetics, environmental factors, and divergent disease drivers. This variability makes it difficult to find effective drugs for all patients with NASH. The drug discovery process generally begins with treating cells in vitro, then moving to in vivo animal models, usually mice, before finally progressing to human clinical trials. A mouse NAFLD/NASH model would be useful if it can mimic the pathogenesis of human NAFLD/NASH. Mouse models are amenable to genetic dissection of complex traits, which helps identify potential genes and pathways for intervention in human beings. However, similar to the heterogeneity of human NAFLD/NASH, pathogenesis of NAFLD also varies significantly in different strains of mice in response to diet. In this issue of Cellular and Molecular Gastroenterology and Hepatology, Hui et al used an elegant hybrid mouse diversity panel that contains more than 100 inbred strains of mice. They used a "systems genetics" approach that integrated clinical and molecular traits with genetic mapping, correlating, and statistical modeling to identify matrix Gla protein (MGP) as a new target for NASH-associated fibrosis.

MGP is a small secretory vitamin K-dependent protein highly expressed by vascular smooth muscle cells and chondrocytes. MGP activates bone morphogenic protein 2 and bone morphogenic protein 4, and acts as a calcification inhibitor in cartilage and vasculature. Homozygous MGP-knockout mice die at approximately 2 months old owing to aberrant cartilage and arterial calcification. Using the global transcriptomic profiling of livers from the hybrid mouse diversity panel, Hui et al found that hepatic expression of Mgp was associated with liver fibrosis in both male and female mice. The expression of Mgp increased with time and correlated with the severity of NASH in mice and NASH patients. Single-cell RNA sequencing analysis revealed that Mgp was highly expressed in HSCs and dendritic cells, and Mergeomics analysis showed that Mgp expression was associated with several connective tissues, ECM genes, and regulators of fibrosis. Intriguingly, female but not male Mgp+/- mice had significantly decreased fibrosis induced by a NASH diet. Mechanistically, loss of MGP in cultured HSCs led to decreased response to transforming growth factor beta owing to increased expression of the inhibitor SMAD6 (Suppressor of Mothers against Decapentaplegic 6), but decreased expression of regulator SMAD and transforming growth factor beta-receptor expression. Together, this study identified MGP as a novel player in HSC activation and liver fibrosis in NASH progression.

Although this study identified MGP as a potential target for liver fibrosis during NASH progression, it has brought up several unanswered questions. One intriguing question is the role of sexual dimorphism in MGP and liver fibrosis. Loss of MGP attenuates fibrosis only in female mice, despite the hepatic expression of Mgp being the same in both genders. Sex hormones do not affect the expression of Mgp in mouse livers, so other risk factors for NASH and liver fibrosis such as intestinal permeability, microbiota, and changes in adipocyte tissues should be investigated in the future. Although the prevalence and severity of NAFLD are higher in men than in women, after menopause, NAFLD occurs at a higher rate in women, suggesting that estrogen is protective in human beings. Further research is required to determine the difference in hepatic expression of MGP between men and women, and whether estrogen has any effect on expression. Although HSCs are the primary source of myofibroblasts that contribute to liver fibrosis, other cell types, such as macrophages and liver sinusoidal endothelial cells, also are important microenvironment components that may contribute to HSC activation and fibrosis. Conducting cell type-specific ablation of MGP in mice could help to further examine its role in the pathogenesis of liver fibrosis. Lastly, there is a need to develop small pharmacologic MGP inhibitors to test the translational value of targeting MGP to fight against liver fibrosis and NASH progression.

passages.text: Cellular stress and coagulation factor production: when more isn't necessarily better

Remarkably, it has been 40 years since the isolation of the two genes involved in hemophilia A (HA) and hemophilia B (HB), encoding clotting factors VIII (FVIII) and IX (FIX), respectively. Over the years these advances led to the development of purified recombinant protein factors that are free of contaminating viruses from human pooled plasma for hemophilia treatments, reducing the morbidity and mortality previously associated with human plasma-derived clotting factors. These discoveries also paved the way to modified factors that have increased plasma half-lives. Importantly, more recent advances have led to development and FDA-approval of a hepatocyte-targeted adeno-associated viral (AAV) vector-mediated gene transfer approach for HA and HB. However, major concerns regarding the durability and safety of HA gene therapy remain to be resolved. Compared to FIX, FVIII is a much larger protein that is prone to misfolding and aggregation in the endoplasmic reticulum and poorly secreted by the mammalian cells. Due to the constraint of the packaging capacity of AAV vector, B domain deleted (BDD) FVIII rather than the full-length protein is used for HA gene therapy. Like full-length FVIII, BDD FVIII misfolds and is inefficiently secreted. Its expression in hepatocytes activates the cellular unfolded protein response, which is deleterious for hepatocyte function, survival, and has the potential to drive hepatocellular carcinoma. This review is focused on our current understanding of factors limiting FVIII secretion and the potential pathophysiological consequences upon expression in hepatocytes.
Introduction

Hemophilia A (HA) and hemophilia B (HB) are caused by deficiencies in clotting factor FVIII (FVIII) and factor IX (FIX), respectively, and represent the most common bleeding disorders. Both FVIII and FIX require proteolytic activation to generate FVIIIa and FIXa that work together to accelerate the conversion of factor X (FX) to FXa in the presence of calcium and negatively charged phospholipids. FVIIIa accelerates FX activation by 6 orders of magnitude in the intrinsic pathway of blood coagulation. HA occurs in 24.6 per 100,000 males at birth whereas there are about 5 cases per 100,000 males for HB. The genes encoding FVIII and FIX are both located on the X chromosome and thus, their defects primarily affect males where females are carriers for the defective FVIII gene. While both types of hemophilia can be fatal, HB is usually less severe than HA. The cloning of the FVIII and FIX genes in the 1980s led to clinical advances in development of recombinant FVIII and FIX protein replacement therapies as well as molecular diagnostics for hemophilia, leading to significantly reduced associated morbidity and mortality. Recombinant factors were free of adventitious viruses (HIV, HCV, and HBV) that were present in plasma-derived factors purified from human pooled plasma donors. However, there were major limitations with these recombinant protein replacement therapies, especially for HA treatment. First, anti-FVIII inhibitory antibodies develop in a significant number (~30%) of patients. Second, recombinant FVIII protein bears a high cost with limited availability due to low and variable production from mammalian host cells, primarily Chinese Hamster Ovary (CHO) or baby hamster kidney cells. Recently, major advances extended the half-lives of these factors in the blood by multiple approaches. Today, the standard of care for HA treatment is prophylactic factor replacement by intravenous infusion at intervals dependent on the T1/2 of the recombinant factor, but generally once/week. Recently, a novel bifunctional monoclonal antibody that reacts with FIXa and FX (Emicizumab) demonstrated significant success as it can be administered subcutaneously every 1-4 weeks and functions in the presence of FVIII inhibitory antibodies.

Adeno-associated viral (AAV) vector-mediated gene transfer of FVIII or FIX to hepatocytes has emerged as a promising therapeutic approach for hemophilia. The success in this therapy led to FDA approval of FIX gene therapy for HB patients. HA gene therapy has also been conditionally approved for use in the European Union and attained full approval by FDA more recently.However, HA gene therapy has encountered two major hurdles: 1) A requirement for very high viral vector doses to drive FVIII expression in hepatocytes; and 2) A decline in therapeutic transgene expression over time accompanied with signs of chronic liver damage, both of which may be directly linked to inefficient FVIII secretion from the cell due to retention, misfolding, and aggregation in the endoplasmic reticulum (ER). Misfolded FVIII activates the unfolded protein response (UPR) that evolved to resolve protein misfolding and reduce cytotoxic effects. This review is focused on our current understanding of factors limiting FVIII secretion and the potential pathophysiological consequences of FVIII expression in hepatocytes.

passages.text: Overview of FVIII, FIX and FV

FVIII is a 330 kDa glycoprotein comprised of six major domains (A1-A2-B-A3-C1-C2) (Figure 1). It circulates in the plasma at a level (0.8 nM) that is at least 10-fold lower than any other clotting factor.

The amino acid (aa) sequences in the A and C domains of FVIII exhibit ~40% aa identity between species, whereas the ~900 aa within the large B domain show no other homology, although it harbors a conserved large number (18) of N-linked oligosaccharides that are observed in the B domains of FVIII from different species, as well as in the homologous clotting factor V (FV), which has the same domain organization of A1-A2-B-A3-C1-C2 as FVIII (Figure 1). The A domains of FVIII share 35-40% aa identity to the A domains of FV and the copper-binding protein ceruloplasmin. The C domains of FVIII and FV also share 35-40% aa identity (Figure 1). There is no significant aa sequence homology between the B domains of FVIII and FV.
FIX is a relatively small protein (57 kDa) composed of four protein domains: -Gla-EGF-EGF-trypsin-like peptidase (Figure 1). Plasma concentrations of FIX are approximately 100-fold higher than FVIII.

The liver is the major site for both FVIII and FIX production. However, while FIX is produced by hepatocytes, FVIII is expressed by sinusoidal endothelial cells and some other endothelial subtypes including human lymphatic endothelial cells, but not by hepatocytes. Besides FVIII, sinusoidal endothelial cells also synthesize von Willebrand factor (VWF), which plays a critical role in stabilizing FVIII in the plasma and maintaining its physiological function
What is B-domain-deleted FVIII?

The mature translation product of full-length human FVIII has 2332 aa. Upon translocation into the ER, FVIII undergoes removal of a 19 aa signal peptide. Upon trafficking to the Golgi compartment, furin-mediated proteolytic cleavage at Arg1313 and/or Arg1648 within the B-domain produces the FVIII heavy chain (A1-a1-A2-a2-N-termial half of B domain) and FVIII light chain (a3-A3-C1-C3) (Figure 2). Lower caps 'a' represent three acidic aa-rich regions that are required for efficient VWF interaction and FXa activation. FVIII circulates in the plasma as a metal bound FVIII heavy chain and light chain-heterodimer in complex with vWF through ionic interactions. During blood coagulation, plasma FVIII is proteolytically activated by FXa or thrombin cleavage at Arg 372 and Arg740 within the heavy chain and at Arg1689 in the light chain, resulting in dissociation from VWF and formation of a heterotrimer (A1/A2/A3-C1-C2), which functions as a cofactor for FIXa to activate FX. As structure-function properties were recently nicely reviewed, we will not discuss structural studies on FVIII here.

Importantly, the B domain-deleted (BDD) FVIII harboring deletion of nearly the entire B-domain (Thr760 - Asp1639) (LA-FVIII, Figure 2) is completely functional, which is similar to Refacto (i.e., SQ-BDD FVIII; Pfizer) that is used as an effective protein replacement therapy for HA patients. The only difference between LA-VIII and SQ-BDD is that SQ-BDD harbors a slightly larger deletion in the B-domain than LA-FVIII (Gln744-Ser1637 vs Thr760 - Asn1639) (Figure 2). A 14-aa linker (SFSQNPPVLKRHQR) at the junction between the A2 and A3 domains in SQ-BDD, termed SQ-linker, preserves the furin-cleavage site at the C-terminus of B domain (i.e., Arg1648). The codon-optimized forms of cDNA encoding SQ-BDD are used in ongoing HA gene therapy clinical studies. SQ-BDD is used for gene therapy because the size of full-length FVIII cDNA is beyond the packaging limit of the AAV genome, which is <5kb. BDD FVIII harbors complete deletion of the B-domain between Arg740 and Glu1649 (BDD or BDD-RE) and is also fully functional (Figure 2).
BiP/GRP78 inhibits FVIII secretion

FVIII has a high tendency to misfold in the ER and is inefficiently secreted in heterologous mammalian cell culture systems. While FV has a similar size and domain organization, it is secreted much more efficiently (up to 10-fold more) than FVIII by CHO cells. The inefficient secretion of FVIII correlates with its binding to the key ER resident chaperone immunoglobulin-binding protein (BiP)/glucose-regulated protein 78 (GRP78). Increased interaction with BiP may lead to requirement for high levels of intracellular ATP for BiP release and FVIII secretion. Unlike FVIII, FV does not associate with BiP and does not require high levels of ATP for secretion. Domain-swapping and deletion analyses of FVIII and FV led to identification of a 110-amino acid region in the FVIII A1 domain (aa 226-336) that inhibits FVIII secretion. Importantly, mutation of Phe at 309 to Ser (F309S), the respective aa residue in FV, in the FVIII A1-domain markedly enhanced secretion of functional FVIII similar to the secretion efficiency of FV, reduced its association with BiP, and decreased its ATP dependence for secretion. The F309S FVIII has a specific activity and thrombin activation profile similar to those of wild-type FVIII but displays increased sensitivity to EDTA-inactivation, which may reflect the observation that F309 is adjacent to C310, a copper ion ligand. F309S mutation may open the copper ion binding pocket to permit metal ion extraction. Previous studies showed that while porcine FVIII has 83% aa sequence identity to human FVIII, recombinant porcine FVIII is expressed at levels 10-100-fold higher than recombinant human FVIII due to its increased secretion efficiency. Along with its efficient secretion, porcine FVIII causes less UPR activation than human FVIII. Importantly, while experimental manipulation of BiP levels exerts a strong reciprocal effect on human FVIII secretion, secretion of porcine FVIII is marginally affected by the level of BiP expression. Taken together, the intrinsic properties of human FVIII associated with its enhanced interaction with BiP may be an important mechanism underlying its poor secretion efficiency.
The Unfolded Protein Response (UPR)

FVIII inefficiently traffics from the ER to the cis-Golgi and its expression in mammalian cells frequently leads to accumulation of unfolded or misfolded FVIII in the ER, which in turn causes ER stress, activates the UPR, and induces cell death.

The UPR is a conserved signaling network evolved to restore ER homeostasis when misfolded proteins accumulate in the ER (Figure 3). In metazoans, the UPR consists of three main pathways: a) Protein kinase RNA (PKR)-like ER Kinase (PERK); b) Inositol-Requiring Enzyme 1 (IRE1); and c) Activating Transcription Factor 6 (ATF6). These ER-localized UPR transducers convey information regarding the intensity and duration of protein misfolding in the ER lumen and transmit signal to the cytosol and nucleus to either adapt and restore proteostasis or undergo cell death or apoptosis in the event of chronic or severe ER stress. Normally, these ER stress transducers are bound to BiP, which inhibits their activation. When protein misfolding occurs in the ER, the misfolded proteins bind and sequester BiP, leading to BiP release from the UPR transducers and triggering UPR activation (Figure 3).
The PERK-eIF2alpha UPR pathway.

PERK is a type 1 transmembrane kinase that is dimerized upon release from BiP for trans-autophosphorylation to phosphorylate the alpha subunit of eukaryotic translation initiation factor 2 (eIF2 alpha) to provide an acute reversible inhibition of protein synthesis. While attenuating global mRNA translation, PERK-eIF2alpha activation paradoxically increases the translation of a selective group of mRNA transcripts, especially the ATF4 mRNA. ATF4 enters the nucleus and activates ER stress response genes that are responsible for the antioxidant response and amino acid biosynthesis and transport to promote cell survival. ATF4 also activates transcription of the growth arrest and DNA damage-inducible protein 34 (GADD34) to induce dephosphorylation of phosphorylated eIF2alpha and restore global mRNA translation. In addition, ATF4 activates transcription of C/EBP homologous protein (CHOP; also known as DDIT3 and GADD153) which plays a crucial role in ER-stress-mediated apoptosis. Chronic ER stress can lead to constitutive PERK-mediated phosphorylation of eIF2alpha to cause apoptosis. However, different cell types may differ in their ability to sustain chronic ER stress to avoid undergoing apoptosis. Furthermore, although CHOP accumulation in the cell correlates with cell death, both ATF4 and CHOP mRNAs and proteins have short half-lives; therefore, a strong and chronic activation of PERK is necessary to increase steady state levels of CHOP to promote cell death.

passages.text: The IRE1alpha-XBP1 UPR pathway.

IRE1, the most conserved UPR signaling pathway across eukaryotes, is a type 1 ER transmembrane protein possessing dual catalytic activities in the cytosolic domain comprising a serine/threonine kinase and a C-terminal endoribonuclease (RNase). Upon release from BiP it is dimerized for trans-autophosphorylation and activation of its RNase activity to initiate unconventional splicing of XBP1 mRNA in the cytoplasm to remove 26 bases from XBP1 mRNA and produce a translational frameshift (Figure 3), leading to synthesis of a potent transcriptional activator XBP1s. In the nucleus, XBP1s regulates expression of its target genes to enhance protein folding, trafficking and ER-associated protein degradation (ERAD) and ER membrane biogenesis to resolve ER protein misfolding. Mammals have two IRE1 genes: ERN1 which encodes IRE1alpha and ERN2 which encodes IRE1beta. ERN1 is ubiquitously and constitutively expressed, whereas ERN2 expression is restricted to intestinal and lung epithelial cells. Chronic IRE1alpha activation also signals apoptosis. Moreover, hyperactivated IRE1alpha cleaves other mRNAs miRNAs, in addition to Xbp1, a process called regulated IRE1-dependent decay (RIDD), but its physiological significance in mammals is yet to be fully understood.
The UPR ATF6 pathway.

ATF6 is a type 2 ER transmembrane protein that contains a cytosolic cAMP-responsive element-binding protein (CREB)/ATF basic leucine zipper (bZIP) domain in its N-terminus. Under non-stressed conditions, ATF6 is retained in the ER through interaction with BiP. Upon UPR activation and release from BiP, ATF6 traffics from the ER to the cis-Golgi apparatus where it is cleaved by Site-1 and Site-2 Proteases (S1P and S2P), generating a cytosolic activated form of ATF6 (ATF6p50), in a process termed regulated intramembrane proteolysis. ATF6p50 then migrates to the nucleus to induce expression of its target genes especially BiP/Grp78 and other key ER chaperone proteins. The main function of ATF6 activation is to mediate the adaptive response to ER protein misfolding by increasing the transcription of genes that increase ER capacity, protein trafficking and ERAD. To date, no substantial evidence supports a direct role of ATF6alpha in ER stress-induced apoptosis.
FVIII folding and secretion: a high expression level does not necessarily lead to more secreted FVIII

Protein aggregate formation in the ER lumen is the most important intrinsic feature of FVIII contributing to its low secretion efficiency by mammalian cells and high propensity to activate the UPR when expressed in vitro or in murine liver in vivo. Protein aggregation is a concentration-dependent event. FVIII exhibits a threshold where it starts to aggregate in the ER and induce ER stress and cell death. In CHO cells (H9) that were engineered to stably express FVIII at a low level under basal conditions, there are no discernible FVIII aggregates in the ER and the UPR is not activated. However, when H9 cells were treated with the histone deacetylase inhibitors sodium butyrate (NaB) or suberoylanilidehydroxamic acid (SAHA) to induce high levels of FVIII mRNA expression, strong activation of all arms of the UPR occurred in a time- and dose-dependent manner, leading to severe ER stress and apoptosis. The most profound changes in UPR signaling in response to high FVIII expression in H9 cells are the dramatically increased levels of BiP, CHOP, and eIF2alpha phosphorylation. The increased BiP level can directly inhibit FVIII anterograde trafficking in the early secretory pathway whereas the excessive eIF2alpha phosphorylation attenuates FVIII synthesis, both of which suppress FVIII secretion. On the other hand, an increase in CHOP expression induces cell death, leading to a complete loss of FVIII production from the affected cells. It is important to emphasize that while NaB treatment of H9 cells increases cellular FVIII synthesis by 10-fold, there was no significant increase in FVIII secretion upon NaB induction. Thus, increased FVIII synthesis does not equate to increased FVIII secretion from the cell. In addition to induction of ER stress, FVIII expression also induces oxidative stress, both in CHO cells in vitro and in murine liver in vivo. Antioxidant treatment reduces UPR activation, oxidative stress, and apoptosis and increases FVIII secretion in vitro and in vivo.

Along with detrimental cellular stress responses induced by high level of FVIII expression in NaB- or SAHA-treated H9 cells, amyloid-like FVIII aggregates accumulated in the ER. Previously, sucrose gradient sedimentation demonstrated newly synthesized FVIII transiently forms aggregates in CHO cells. Recently, we demonstrated upon high level expression, FVIII forms amyloid-like fibrils in the ER by several approaches: a) FVIII co-localized with the amyloid-specific dye Thioflavin-S (Thio-S); b) Immuno-gold transmission electron microscopy demonstrated FVIII clustering with the ER-localized PDIA6; c) Cryo-EM demonstrated FVIII purified from NaB-treated H9 cells forms ~5nm fibrils; d) The FVIII amyloids were sensitive to 1% SDS, however, a small fraction (~3%) was resistant, similar to other well-characterized amyloids; and e) These amyloid-like fibrils do not bind BiP, suggesting they are in a highly aggregated state.

Interestingly, formation of FVIII amyloid in the ER is a glucose-regulated and reversible cellular event. Depletion of ER ATP by inhibition of glycolysis with 2-deoxyglucose, but not oxidative phosphorylation, exacerbates FVIII aggregation. However, aggregated FVIII can partially refold to its native folding state and be secreted as biologically functional FVIII when normal glucose metabolism is restored. To the best of our knowledge, this is the first example that an aggregated protein can disaggregate, fold properly and be secreted in metazoan cells.

Proteomics analysis of intracellular FVIII protein complex isolated from NaB-induced H9 cells demonstrated BiP and calnexin/calreticulin are key chaperone proteins that interact with FVIII, all of which prevent FVIII aggregation in the ER. Specifically, acute disruption of BiP function in NaB-induced H9 cells by treatment with Subtilase toxin (SubAB) to cleave and inactivate BiP increased FVIII aggregation in H9 cells with normal glucose metabolism. Conversely, SubAB-mediated acute inactivation of BiP prevented dissociation of FVIII aggregates in the energy-depleted NaB-induced H9 cells in response to restoration of glucose metabolism. These observations are consistent with the role of BiP as a major ER chaperone, which mainly functions in the ER by binding to newly synthesized client proteins to maintain their folding-competent state and interacting with its misfolded client proteins to prevent protein aggregation. However, release of client proteins from BiP-client protein complexes requires ATP consumption and excessive or aberrant BiP-client protein interactions may hamper exit of client proteins from the ER for secretion. As discussed earlier, a number of studies previously established that BiP inhibits FVIII secretion. The enhanced interaction between BiP and FVIII may lead to a higher energy demand to support FVIII secretion. Further studies are required to understand how BiP exerts its inhibitory effect on FVIII secretion while it functions to facilitate FVIII folding.

Compared to FVIII, clotting factor V (FV) was efficiently secreted and did not bind BiP, although they have similar domain structures. Previous studies using chimeric FVIII and FV cDNA molecules identified a 110-aa region (aa 226-336) within the FVIII A1 domain as the FVIII peptide region that interacts with BiP and mediates the inhibitory effect of BiP on FVIII secretion. Recently, a 79-aa region (aa 253-336, FVIII253-336) within this 110-aa peptide region was shown to contain the necessary domains responsible for FVIII aggregation and BiP-binding. A fusion protein containing FVIII253-336-eGFP-proinsulin C peptide aggregated and misfolded in a similar manner as full-length FVIII. It was subsequently demonstrated that a short hydrophobic motif within this 97-aa region, residues 298-309, is necessary and sufficient to seed beta-sheet polymerization and promote FVIII aggregation. As with the full-length FVIII, mutation of F309S also attenuated aggregation of the FVIII253-336-eGFP-proinsulin C peptide fusion protein and its interaction with BiP. Thus, the aa 298-309 of FVIII may be the minimal domain required for FVIII aggregation.

An outstanding question is whether amyloid-like BDD FVIII aggregates are present in hepatocytes of the AAV-FVIII-transduced livers in vivo in the setting of gene therapy. In addition, while it was shown that increases in the full-length FVIII expression and synthesis do not necessarily lead to a corresponding increase in FVIII secretion by the host cells, this phenomenon has not been reported in the literature regarding BDD secretion. Nevertheless, numerous studies have shown that like the full-length FVIII, BDD expression activates the UPR signaling and induces detrimental cellular responses in the host cells. Importantly, ectopic expression of SQ-BDD in human primary hepatocytes also elicits UPR activation and induces ER stress, including induction of BiP expression and increased eIF2alpha phosphorylation.

Codon-optimized human SQ-BDD cDNA, rather than the wild-type SQ-BDD cDNA, is used for most the preclinical trials and all clinical trials for AAV-mediated liver-targeted HA gene therapy. Codon optimization in this setting may increase mRNA expression and/or translation of SQ-BDD cDNA. Improvements in SQ-BDD FVIII secretion at the magnitude of >10 fold have been achieved from codon-optimized SQ-BDD cDNA vs the wild type SQ-BDD cDNA. Even with the AAV vectors harboring codon-optimized SQ-BDD cDNA, plasma FVIII levels in mice and human subjects after AAV-transduction were increased in a vector dose-dependent manner. These observations raise a possibility that in the setting of gene therapy, increases in SQ-BDD synthesis may generally lead to increased SQ-BDD output from the AAV-SQ-BDD-transduced livers. However, further investigations are needed to understand the hepatocyte cellular response and the pathological consequences associated with high levels of SQ-BDD expression in hepatocytes.
Pathophysiological consequence of ectopic FVIII expression in hepatocytes

Hydrodynamic Tail vein injection of vector DNA (HTD) was used to express full length and BDD FVIII in the murine hepatocytes and study the pathophysiological effect of FVIII and BDD in the liver. Expression of FVIII or BDD in hepatocytes activated the UPR and markedly increased hepatic levels of BiP, eIF2alpha phosphorylation and CHOP, leading to hepatocyte death in a CHOP-dependent manner. FVIII and BDD expression also increased hepatic level of reactive oxygen species and caused oxidative stress in the liver. Treatment of the mice that received FVIII or BDD expression vector DNA with antioxidants, especially butylated hydroxyanisole, improved FVIII and BDD secretion, alleviated ER stress and prevented cell death (Figure 4A). N-linked glycosylation modification of FVIII plays a critical role in FVIII folding and secretion. Beside BDD, we generated a partial B domain deletion molecule, herein N6, that retains an additional 226 aa with 6 N-linked glycosylation sites from the N-terminal portion of the B domain (Figure 4A), and is secreted ~10-fold more efficiently than full-length FVIII or BDD, presumably due to the 6 N-glycans that engage the intracellular lectin chaperone machinery, demonstrated to enhance FVIII trafficking from the ER to the Golgi compartment. Unlike full-length FVIII and BDD, HTD-mediated ectopic expression of N6 in murine hepatocytes in vivo minimally activated the UPR and did not cause oxidative stress and thus, N6 secretion was not responsive to antioxidant treatment (Figure 4A).

As BiP binding plays a particularly important role in FVIII folding and secretion, we used a recently generated genetically modified mouse harboring a conditional floxed 3x FLAG tag inserted into the endogenous BiP/GRP78/Hspa5 locus (BiP-Flag mice) to gain further insights into the folding status of BDD and N6 ectopically expressed in hepatocytes, which allows for quantitative analysis of BiP-client protein interaction through FLAG-pull down assays. Interactions between BiP-Flag and BDD or N6 were measured by analyzing anti-FLAG co-immunoprecipitation (IP) of BDD and N6. We found that 2-3 times more BDD than N6 was pulled down by FLAG IP from the liver lysates of these mice. These results support the notion that BDD exhibits greater misfolding than N6 in hepatocytes of murine livers, which likely accounts for the different degrees of induction of the UPR.

To determine if amyloid-like FVIII aggregates are present in the BDD- or N6-expressing livers, we performed hFVIII and Thio-S staining on the liver sections of mice that received BDD or N6 expression vector DNA. Strong Thio-S staining that colocalized with hFVIII stain was observed in the liver sections of BDD vector DNA-injected mice. In contrast, while strong FVIII staining was observed in the sections of livers of mice injected with N6 DNA vector, very little signal for Thio-S stain was found, further confirming that N6 FVIII folds more efficiently than BDD in vivo in hepatocytes. These results for the first time, provide evidence demonstrating ectopic expression of BDD in hepatocytes in vivo leads to intracellular accumulation of amyloid-like FVIII aggregates in the liver, which in turn activates the UPR signaling and causes cytotoxic responses in the liver.

passages.text: Previously, we demonstrated high-fat diet (HFD) feeding to mice that transiently over-express urokinase-type plasminogen activator in hepatocytes from a hepatocyte-specific transgene, which misfolds in the ER, initiates development of non-alcoholic steatohepatitis and hepatocellular carcinomas (HCC) while HFD feeding alone does not induce HCC, raising a possibility that transient hepatocyte expression of FVIII molecules with different folding efficiencies in the ER may also promote HCC in mice. To address this question, we delivered BDD and N6 expression vectors to murine livers by HTD. The mice that received the parental DNA vector expressing dihydrofolate reductase (DHFR) served as negative control. All of these mice were then fed a 60% HFD for 65 weeks starting at one week after plasmid DNA injection when FVIII expression was undetectable. Greater tumor formation was observed in BDD vector-injected mice than N6 vector-injected mice (100% vs 58%, p=0.02). Both HCC and adenomas were found in the mice. Importantly, none of the mice that received the parental DHFR vector DNA developed liver tumors, indicating that liver tumor development in the BDD or N6 vector-injected mice was not due to transient liver cell injury caused by HTD. Together, these findings support the notion that the degree of ER protein misfolding may be a significant factor in liver disease progression (Figure 4B). Our findings also point to a potential risk regarding ectopic expression of FVIII in hepatocytes in the context of HA gene therapy.

The connection between gene transfer to hepatocytes, liver function, and HCC has recently become a very highly debated issue and previous studies have demonstrated delivery of AAV vector to hepatocytes alone can induce HCC. In our study, plasmid DNA tail vein injection was used to achieve BDD and N6 expression in the murine liver and thus, avoiding the confounding factor of AAV vector integration and its direct carcinogenic effect. Analysis of DNA isolated from tumor tissues of our mice obtained through micro-dissection revealed that none of the tumors found in our mice expressed BDD or N6, providing further evidence supporting the notion that transient expression of misfolded FVIII in hepatocytes in combination with subsequent HFD feeding is sufficient to induce HCC. It is of great importance to investigate if the amount of SQ-BDD produced by hepatocytes under a setting of AAV gene transfer reaches a threshold required to set off the cascade of molecular events that promotes HCC.

While AAV-SQ-BDD gene transfer has not been found to cause the level of hepatocyte apoptosis and liver injury that may occur with HTD-mediated DNA vector delivery, multiple studies have shown induction of ER stress markers in mice in response to AAV-SQ-BDD transduction. Signs of liver injury, including elevated liver enzyme levels, were observed in patients treated with high-dose AAV-SQ-BDD. Furthermore, FVIII expression levels gradually declined to the lower end of the therapeutic range, starting in the second year. While immune response to the AAV vector is known to play an important role in liver pathology and the decline in SQ-BDD expression in the clinical setting,, it is possible that SQ-BDD misfolding and UPR activation impact hepatocyte function, health, and/or survival. Recently, Butterfield et al developed a preclinical FVIII-deficient HA mouse model that exhibits declining SQ-BDD expression upon AAV8-SQ-BDD transduction similar to that observed in HA clinical trials. Intriguingly, it was found that FVIII expression declined despite persistence of the therapeutic FVIII transgene and SQ-BDD mRNA, suggesting that a translational block rather than loss of transduced hepatocytes or transcriptional repression is responsible for decline in plasma FVIII level in this mouse model. Elevated levels of eIF2alpha phosphorylation was observed in the livers of these AAV8-SQ-BDD transduced mice, suggesting that activation of PERK-eIF2alpha arm of the UPR signaling may play a role in inhibition of FVIII translation in this mouse model, the same pathway that limited early mRNA vaccine designs. Elevated eIF2alpha phosphorylation correlated with inflammatory cytokine expression in the liver and negatively correlated with FVIII activity in circulation. Independent of immune suppression, approximately half of transduced mouse livers showed evidence for development of cellular stress. Thus, cellular stress/UPR activation, inflammation, and FVIII protein production are likely interconnected. Results from this mouse study and biopsies obtained from livers of patients who had received AAV-FVIII gene transfer agree that decline in expression did not result from a destructive immune response since transduced hepatocytes persisted at high level. To further complicate matters, AAV vector genomes that are somewhat larger than that of the wild-type virus ("oversized vectors"), as is typical for AAV-FVIII, may be prone to transcriptional silencing over time because of epigenetic changes that decreased vector genome accessibility. These multifactorial influences on transcription and translation (derived from biology of the vector, ectopic FVIII expression and the immune system) complicate the quest for sustained gene therapy for hemophilia A. Limiting expression per hepatocytes and spreading expression over many hepatocytes (through choice of promoter/expression cassette design and choice of viral capsid and adjusted vector dose), immune modulation, and possibly employment of FVIII variants with improved secretion may help accomplish this goal.

Protein engineering to enhance the folding and secretion efficiency of FVIII molecules used for HA gene therapy may be a fruitful approach to developing a safer, more effective, and durable HA gene therapy. While the F309S mutation remarkably improved full-length FVIII folding and secretion, its potential to improve SQ-BDD secretion and reduce the cytotoxic response induced by FVIII expression has not been investigated adequately. On the other hand, porcine FVIII is secreted 10-fold more efficiently than human FVIII. By comparing human and porcine FVIII aa sequences, which share ~65% aa identify excluding the B domain, Cao et al discovered that exchange of 5 aa in the A1 domain (X5-SQ-BDD) from human to porcine aa improved secretion by ~10-fold, suggesting that X5-SQ-BDD may be a promising FVIII molecule for HA gene therapy. Currently, little is known about the mechanism underlying the improved secretion efficiency of X5-SQ-BDD and its folding properties in the ER.

passages.text: The post-translational processing of single chain FVIII involving furin cleavages at Arg1311 and Arg1648 is believed to play a crucial role in secretion and function of human FVIII, leading to the development of a modified version of SQ-linker for SQ-BDD to enhance furin-mediated proteolytic cleavage at Arg1648. Nevertheless, while canine FVIII does not contain the corresponding furin-cleavage motif, the recombinant canine SQ-BDD, which is efficiently secreted mainly as a single-chain protein, is more stable and has higher biological activity than human SQ-BDD. Consequently, hepatic gene transfer using relatively low vector doses of AAV vectors expressing canine BDD-FVIII (without codon-optimization) was sufficient to produce life-long correction of the bleeding disorder in dogs with HA., indicating the high efficiency of canine BDD-FVIII in HA gene therapy. A series of studies using various mutant forms of human SQ-BDD engineered to avoid furin cleavage at Arg 1648 uniformly showed that circumventing furin-mediated proteolytic cleavage actually increased SQ-BDD yield and FVIII activity 3-fold from both mammalian cell culture and after AAV-based gene therapy in small and large-animal HA models. Currently, it is not known whether preventing furin processing of SQ-BDD at Arg 1648 improves SQ-BDD secretion or increases its stability, intracellularly and/or extracellularly. An interesting question remaining to answer is whether a complete elimination of SQ-linker in SQ-BDD would further enhance FVIII expression in HA gene therapy.
Concluding Remarks

Significant discoveries after isolation of the clotting factor genes in the mid 1980's include key progress in our in-depth understanding of the folding and secretion of FVIII and FIX. FVIII and FIX protein replacement therapy for hemophilia has been significantly improved. However, there is still need for the long-term goal of a 'lifetime' cure for hemophilia. Intriguingly, different responses to hepatocyte-targeted AAV-mediated gene therapy of FVIII and FIX have been noted. Several differences may account for the delayed approval of AAV-FVIII therapy. First, as FVIII is about 5x the size of FIX, AAV preparations have used a BDD FVIII variant due to size packaging constraints of the AAV vector. Second, FVIII has significant challenges for protein folding and modification in the ER of the mammalian cells. Its expression in hepatocytes activates UPR, which is deleterious for hepatocyte function, survival, and has the potential to drive hepatocellular carcinoma. In addition, while hepatocytes are the natural site for FIX production, FVIII is primarily expressed in sinusoidal endothelial cells. A further understanding of these differences may yield discoveries that increase stability and safety of AAV-FVIII gene therapy. While improvement in AAV vector design and production and further studies on immunological responses to AAV transduction will play an important role in improving HA gene therapy, bioengineering studies to improve FVIII folding, secretion, and activity will likely be a key area for future study. Furthermore, more in-depth studies into the long-term safety of ectopic FVIII expression in hepatocytes will produce crucial information for the long-term goal of developing a permanent cure of HA, which should be achieved within the next 10 years.
